headline: A train hit a stopped train in Spain. At least 69 died.
summary: A high-speed train from Madrid to Seville ran into a stopped train on Wednesday morning, 140km south of Madrid. At least 69 people died. A computer failure had halted the trains. Recordings show a control centre then told the driver to go on at normal speed. Spain began three days of mourning, and its train drivers struck on Thursday.
cover_answer: Very rarely. A signal failed in Spain, far from here.
table_question: When a machine fails and a person then errs, who carries the blame?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: Two trains crashed into each other in Spain on Wednesday, far away across the ocean. A lot of people were hurt and some died. Trains follow signals the way cars follow traffic lights, and a signal went wrong. The grown-ups in Spain are finding out exactly what happened, so they can fix it.
5-7.why: Only if it comes up. Far away, a reason, and someone fixing it.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, so the first move is distance: Spain, across an ocean. The second is a mechanism they trust, the traffic light, because what frightens this age is a thing with no reason, and a signal that broke is a reason. Expect "could our train crash?" Very rarely, and the grown-ups have it.

8-12.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
8-12.script: On Wednesday morning a high-speed train from Madrid to Seville ran into a train stopped on the track ahead. At least 69 people died. Trains run on signals the way cars run on traffic lights: a computer failed, six trains stopped, and a control centre told one driver to go again at normal speed.
8-12.why: Computer failed, control room said go, normal speed. One chain.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out chains of cause and effect, so the script hands them one: a computer failed, six trains stopped, a control centre said go, at normal speed. The traffic light shows where the chain broke. Expect "whose fault was it?" The minister calls the order inexplicable; Podemos says it must not land on one worker.

13-17.script: When a computer fails and then a person does, who is to blame? A computer failure halted six trains in Spain. Recordings show the control centre then told a driver to go on at normal speed, and he hit a stopped train. Second: 46 died on this line in January. Is twice a system failure?
13-17.why: Machine error, then human error. Let them argue who owns it.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can reason about a system they cannot see, so the script hands them the chain and two readings of it: one control-room order, or a railway that let one order become 69 deaths. Kuhn's point: argument is practised against someone who argues back, so take a side. Expect "will anyone resign?" Protesters want the minister out.

5-7.a: Trains crash very rarely. This one happened because a signal went wrong far away in Spain, and the grown-ups there are fixing it.

8-12.q: How can a train hit a stopped one?
8-12.a: A computer failed, then a control room said go at normal speed.
The prime minister promised to, and to fix any safety failure.

13-17.a: Both: the computer failed, then the control room said go.

13-17.q: Why does the election matter here?
13-17.a: Spain votes November 29. Vox won't let mourning gag criticism.
